🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.97% (intraday, 7-year -14bp). At trading day 48 (last close) it was +0.79% against a five-campaign average of -1.32% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -1.19%. The 10-year is -9bp since the hike vs a +21bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 802bp against a five-year average of 423bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +38bp and BB +6bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.35 → 0.69 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.69). Investment grade is untouched (+5bp).
  • AI Credit: CoreWeave 5Y CDS 1,211bp, -112bp since 2026-11-23, through the Oct 15 record — the market is not buying Nvidia's backstop. Its June 9.625% 2032s are at 78.4 (15.5%, -0.4pts in a month). Up the stack: Nvidia 142bp, Oracle 347bp. Neocloud stocks 1m: CRWV -11%, NBIS -38%, IREN -41% vs NVDA -22%.
  • Tech Phase: Phase 1 of the 2000 template, day 35 after the tech basket's 2026-10-06 peak: basket -25.7% vs -18.3% for 2000 on the same day. Model odds of being in spread widening or worse: 50% in 3m, 44% in 6m; odds spreads cross the Phase-2 line at some point within 12m: 90%. 6m odds +8.6pp since 2026-11-23. Triggered signposts: CoreWeave 5Y CDS; VXN (Nasdaq vol); Basket names >20% off high; SOX.
  • Stocks: Tech fell hard while old-economy blue chips rose; the Dow closed above 50,000.
  • FX: The dollar eased; the yen stayed near 159, a level that invites intervention.
  • Technicals: Stocks trade below their 50- and 200-day averages, so trends are weak and stretched.
  • Sectors: Money moved into health care and staples and out of technology.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lowest-rated junk debt is the most stressed since 2020, and single-B is now widening too.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is elevated: weak spots are AI borrowers and the lowest-rated companies.
  • Inflation: Sticky core prices keep inflation above target even though markets expect it to cool.
  • Tech Bubble: Tech is in an early bust phase; the model sees worse odds ahead.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Dell reports tonight with a huge expected move; Anthropic's mega-IPO tests demand.
  • Iran: Ceasefire talks and attacks on Hormuz shipping continue; we found nothing dated today.
  • Warsh: Warsh is biased toward hikes but data-dependent; a December move is uncertain.
  • Week Ahead: Short Thanksgiving week: GDP/PCE data, then Marvell and Okta earnings on December 1.
  • Outlook: Cautious short term: AI-credit stress must ease before any rally can be trusted.
  • Trades: Favor Treasuries and gold, cut Nasdaq exposure, avoid the lowest-rated junk bonds.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 4 hold long, 41 stay out

  • Bottom line: The AI unwind is spreading into credit; stay defensive until credit stops widening.

The biggest story of the session is a sharp split inside US equities. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.477902% to 23733.54 and the S&P 500 fell 0.4985374% to 7201.09, while the Dow rose 0.8536896% to 50018.7 and the Russell 2000 rose 0.5726208%. Info Tech lost 2.77% on the day and is down 14.47% over one month. Health Care gained 2.88% and Staples 1.73%. That is a classic rotation out of AI leadership and into defensives, not broad risk-off: VIX actually slipped to 26.36 from 26.62. Abroad, the Euro Stoxx 50 fell 1.164052% and the Nikkei jumped 3.912316% as JGB 10Y yields fell 6.8bp to 2.732%. Credit is the part that matters. In US high yield, the Caa–B gap is 802bp, at the 99.84th percentile of the last five years. It is up 198bp in three months, and the CCC tier is the widest since 2020-04-15. The question is whether that stress is spreading up the ladder. Single-B OAS is 362bp, up 41bp in a week and 38bp in a month. The B–Ba gap is at 151bp, the 78th percentile of five years. Ba (+6bp in a month) and IG (94bp, +6bp in a week) are still mostly holding. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has climbed from 0.35 three months ago to 0.69, back to its five-year median. So the CCC rot is visibly spreading into single-B, but not yet decisively into BB or investment grade. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. The AI-credit backstop question remains open. CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1210.6bp. That is 16.1bp above the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record and more than 100% of the June-low-to-record run, even after a 112.4bp tightening versus yesterday. Nvidia CDS eased 7.17bp to 142.21bp but is still 13.49bp wider on the week, and Nvidia's DRSK model-implied CDS sits at its 1-year high (100th percentile). The tape says the market is not yet fully buying Nvidia's backstop of the neoclouds. Stress is migrating toward the guarantor rather than being absorbed by it. CoreWeave equity is about 65% below its 52-week high and IREN about 78% below. CDX HY is at 374.8bp, the 97.2nd percentile of the past year. This too is descriptive, not a validated signal. The tech phase model still places us in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm). Four signposts have triggered: CoreWeave CDS through its record, VXN at 36.49 (above 35), 78.6% of basket names more than 20% off their highs, and the SOX 39.65% off its 52-week high. The model's 6-month Phase 2+3 odds rose 8.6 percentage points versus the prior run, and its 12-month 'ever Phase 2 or worse' odds rose 20.1 points to 0.898. These are model estimates, not certainties. The defensive dial stays at Step 1, Cautious. Versus the prior session, sentiment has shifted from a broad AI sell-off to a rotation with a credit undertow. Net: cautious, with credit as the arbiter.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 370.30 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD sits at 370.3 cents/gal, at the 97.3rd percentile of its history (z 2.13), and every card points SELL. Refining margins are the most stretched of the five, with the crack at 73.476 $/bbl (98.6th percentile, z 3.58). Because all of the strength is in the front months and the margin, mean reversion is the base case, but the wide stops show how violently past squeezes have run before they turned.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.22 vol points (3th percentile of the 77 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 98.8 (71th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 66bp (flatter by 20bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 54 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 63/100 — Inflation is persistent at the core but narrowing in breadth. Underlying measures sit above target and mostly rising versus their history: Median CPI 2.8%, 16% Trimmed-Mean CPI 2.9%, Core Sticky CPI 3.06%, and Core PCE YoY 3.12%. The computed core-trend sub-score is rendered separately. Breadth is mixed. Dallas Fed data show 16.6% of the PCE basket inflating above 10% and 10.2% at 5–10%, but 25.6% of the basket is falling. Market pricing disagrees with the sticky core: the 1y breakeven is 1.7365% and the 5y breakeven 2.1496%, consistent with the growth scare and lower oil versus its averages. Wages are not the driver: average hourly earnings are 3.1% and ECI YoY is 0.8%. Verdict: sticky enough to keep a hiking-biased Fed on hold or tightening, but not re-accelerating broadly.

BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
10 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 6 beyond 2000 — 60/100
Today rhymes more with the early 2000–2001 bust than with the March 2000 peak. - **Equity Froth has deflated:** the Nasdaq is 5.7% below its 200DMA (0% of the 2000 stretch), and SOX P/E 30.27x is 26% of the 2000 peak. Nasdaq trailing P/E is n/a. - **Late-cycle catalyst readings are at or past 2000 conditions:** IG at 122% of 2000 tightness, Baa–10Y at 148%, NFCI at 151%, commodities-vs-equities at 200%. - **The curve has not inverted:** 2s10s is +24.68bp (72%). - **Sentiment has already broken:** AAII -8.9 (27%), VIX 26.4 (52%). The phase model puts the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm). It is 35 days from peak, with a basket drawdown of -25.72% versus -18.34% for 2000 on the same day. The model's odds are model estimates, not certainties: - **6 months:** P1 0.28, P2 0.331, P3 0.104, P4 0.285. - **12 months:** P4 (trough/healing) 0.437; ever reaching Phase 2 or worse 0.898. The closest historical path is 1997 Asia (NDX -9.6% on day 35 versus -16.0% now), but the Fed is hiking now as in 1999/2000, not holding as in 1997/1998. Recovery signposts: 0 of 5.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle
IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The dot-com analogy has moved from 'are we at the peak?' to 'how deep is the bust?'. Price froth has already been washed out of the Nasdaq (-16.05% from its 52-week high) and the SOX (-39.65% from its high). What has not been washed out is credit complacency in the broad indices. IG at 0.94% and Baa–10Y are tighter than at the 2000 peak, and financial conditions (NFCI -0.48) are looser. Meanwhile the speculative edge of AI credit is cracking: CoreWeave CDS sits above its record and CCC spreads are at five-year extremes. In 2000–01 the move from Phase 1 to Phase 2 came when credit widening spread from the weakest names to the broad HY index. That is the transition the model's HY signposts (448bp and 420bp) are watching. The IPO market adds a late-mania flavour. Renaissance Capital estimated a $75bn+ Anthropic listing after SpaceX's roughly $75bn June IPO. Mega-listings of this size during a drawdown are a supply signal reminiscent of 1999–2000. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 concentration, CAPE, market-cap/GDP, LT EPS-growth froth, IPO froth) are approximate. We did not verify them via web search this run and they should be treated as rough.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

December FOMC: we lean toward a hold with a hawkish bias, and a hike is a live risk (inference). Warsh has said the September hike is 'having its intended effect'. He has also avoided forward guidance and stressed that 'more information will help determine' policy. Three dissenters (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) favored a hike at the last meeting. Core PCE of 3.12% supports the hawks. The equity drawdown, CCC credit stress and 1y breakevens of 1.7365% argue for patience. The 2Y yield at 4.6829% is consistent with a market not pricing an aggressive hiking path.

~1 YEAR

~1 year: a price-stability-first Fed that tolerates tighter policy. Warsh's Jackson Hole framing ('at sufficient speed') leaves room to hike even while inflation falls, and his October remarks tied the AI investment surge to inflation pressure. Commentators also expect balance-sheet reduction and institutional reforms. We infer one to two further hikes are possible if core stays above 3%. A pivot to cuts would most likely require a credit event (e.g. the HY contagion reaching BB/IG). This is inference, not on-record guidance.

Warsh took the chair in May and delivered the Fed's first hike in three years in September, by a unanimous vote. Since then he has held, while emphasising resilience and declining to pre-commit. His record and writings point to price-stability primacy, scepticism of forward guidance, and a smaller balance sheet. Our search found no verified November remark signalling a December move. The near-term call above is therefore inferred from on-record statements up to mid-October. Note that the sources disagree on the exact policy range, so we quote no range here.
